function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I don’t have the ability to run shell commands, clone repositories, or push commits from here.  
What I can do is give you the exact files you’ll need to add to the repository, along with a short script‑style guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal to finish the job locally.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository (run this yourself)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and don’t have SSH set up, you can also clone via HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate the required files

Below are the minimal Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow that match a typical Node.js “Hello World” app.  
Feel free to tweak the values (e.g., image tags, replica counts) to suit your environment.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes only what’s needed for production.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from the lockfile.  
> * The `CMD` matches the typical entrypoint for a simple Node app (`node app.js`).  

If the repo already contains a Dockerfile that differs from this, replace it with the above or merge the relevant parts.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or split into separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`) with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                 # External port
    targetPort: 3000         # Container port
```

> **How to use it**  
> ```bash
> kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
> ```

Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the actual registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`).

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image using the Dockerfile in the repo.  
> * Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry under the same name as the repo.  

Make sure the repository has the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (it’s automatically available in Actions). If you want to push to another registry, adjust the login step accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

If you replaced an existing Dockerfile, you might want to stage the old one for review:

```bash
git add -u Dockerfile
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Optional** – If you’re on a feature branch and want to merge into `main`:

```bash
git checkout main
git pull
git merge feature-branch-name
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new workflow run in the **Actions** tab of the GitHub repo.  
* The Docker image `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` appearing in the **Packages** section.  
* Running `kubectl get deployments` should show `nodejs-welcome-deployment` with 2 ready replicas (once you’ve applied the manifest).

That’s it! Let me know if you hit any snags while applying these steps.
